full_judgment:
2. Facts are as follows: Late Digindra Chandra Bhattacharya the predecessor of the appellants instituted a suit being Probate Suit No. 5 of 1974 for grant of Probate in respect of the last will dated 30.12.62 executed by Kitish Chandra Bhattacharya. In the said will the testator appointed his step-mother Jalada Debi, the respondent in this appeal as the first executor subject to the condition that in case first executrix failed to take Probate the second executor Digindra Chandra Bhattacharya would be entitled to take Probate and became the sole legatee in respect of the properties bequeathed under the said will. 

 5. A review application was filed under Order 47 read with section 151 C.P.C. which was numbered as Misc. Case No. 29 of 1980 It may be noted that when the order in O.C. Suit No. 71 of 1975 was passed the F. A. No. 101 of 1976 was still pending. Being aggrieved by the order in O.C. Suit No.7 of 1975 the Misc. Case No 29 of 1981 wall filed which, however, was rejected on 20.2.80. Thereafter C.R. No. 37 of 1981 was filed before the District Judge Mymensingh. 

 From the above narration of facts as mentioned above it is clear that Jalada Devi initially intended to take probate but when it was found contentious her application was returned to her. She instead of filing a regular suit started disposing all the properties which necessitated a suit for injunction by Digindra. In that injunction suit Jalada for the first time took the stand that the Will was forged. That amounts to her refusal to act as an executor. In the Will it is mentioned that if Jalada dies then Digiudra will be the second executor. That led Digindra to file the Probate suit because Jalada refused to act. Now the contention whether Jalada is dead or alive has led to another set of litigation being O.C. suit No. 71 of 1975 and by order dated 8.9.71 it was found by the learned Additional District Judge that Jalada is no more alive. Until this order h set aside then position remains that Digindra being the next executor was competent to file the Probate suit but Digihdra also died. His two sons filed application for substitution. This petition was refused by order dated 5.4.76 which led to the F.A. No. 101 of 1976. With respect, the learned Judges of the High Court Division have not correctly approached the facts of the case. In the O.C. Suit No.71 of 1975 it was found that Jalada is no more alive and until this finding is set aside by the superior court no contrary assumption can be made by another court while dealing with another subject matter namely whether the heirs of Digindra could be substituted. Numerous adjournments were taken from this court to thrash out the controversy whether Jalada is dead or alive and the C.R.No.37 of 1981 (arising out of O.C. Suit No. 71 of 1975) is stil pending. The learned Judge in the F. A. had erroneously travelled into the path which had unfortunately led them to a blind alley. The position is that, Jalada is dead or alive, had refused to act on the ground that the will itself was forged one. It need not detain us whether she approbated or reprobated in this matter. The clear position emerges is that she refused to act as executor. Section 232(b) reads as follows: 

 In such case an universal or residuary legatee may be allowed to prove the will and letter of administer that the will annexed may be granted to him. Since Jalada refused to act as executor the petition for Probate by Digindra was competent. The question is when Digindra died, whether his sons could be substituted. The courts below have found section 222 as a bar which reads as under: 

 When the first executor refused to act the second executor could legitimately file the petition for probate. The nature of the proceeding in a probate suit may be considered. An executor when applies for a probate of the Will of the deceased testator merely asks the court for order in his favour to the effect that the will is duly proved and to administer the estate of the deceased according to the provision contained in the will. As. executor he has no personal interest in the Estate of the deceased but if he is a legatee under the will then a new dimension is added. The object of the executor is to propound the will of the deceased for the benefit of those who take the interest of the will. Thus the maxim action personalis moritor cum persona has no manner of application in such case. For it is in substance not a personal action. In substance Probate means copy of the will certified under the seal of a Court of competent jurisdiction that a grant of administration to the Esatate of Testator vide the definition of Probate in section 2 of the Succession Act. In the absence of an executor an universal or residuary legatee can apply for letter of administration and what the Court grants in such a case is also a copy of the Will certified under the seal of the Court stating that the will is only duly approved and an authority to administer the estate of the deceased according to the direction. In substance the fact of the grant is more or less same. It is true that an executor gets his preferential right to the grant from nomination in the will. While in the other case the grant is by reason of the Court. In either of the cases purpose of the grant is to administer of the estate of the deceased according to the provision of the will. In the will in question Digindra has been nominated as second executor and if Jalada refuses to act or dies Digindra will take the Probate and the will says “তদাবস্থায় তিনি আমার ত্যাক্ত স্থাবর সম্পত্তি নিবিড় স্বত্ব প্রাপ্ত হইবেন।” In this context the question is whether the heirs of Digindra should be substituted. 

 8. Apparently there are divergent authorities on this point. In Sarat Chandra Banerjee Vs. Nani Mohan Banerjee, 36 cal. 799 Harrington J. held that on the death of the sole executor pending the hearing of the probate suit, the right to sue does not survive in favour of his legal representatives. It was pointed out in that case that executor's right to probate was a personal right derived not from an order of the court but from appointment made by the testator himself whereas the right to be appointed by the Court to administer the assets of the deceased stands on different footing. This decision was not however, followed by the Calcutta High Court in the subsequent cases. In the case of Haripada Saha and another Vs Gobinda Chandra Saha and ors 51 C W.N 917 the dictum passed in the aforesaid case has somewhat been watered down. In the case of Haripada Saha, Subasini was appointed a sole executrix under the will. She filed an application for probate of the Will and 6 days later she died. Her heirs made an application before the District Delegate praying for permission to continue the proceeding as substituted heirs in place of Subasini and they prayed that letters of administration with a copy of the will annexed may be granted to them. A Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court considered the objection as technical and observed: 

 There is undoubtedly a technical defect, but it is not a defect which has in any way affected the merits of the case of the jurisdiction of the Court". 

 The Patna High Court, on the other hand, took a firm view. In the case of Mt. Phekni Vs. Mt. Manki, A.I.R.1930 Patna 618 took the view that where the sole legatee under will whose application for grant of letters of administration is rejected appeals from the order, but dies during the pendency of the appeal, the heirs of the sole legatee can be substituted in his place for the purpose of carrying on the litigation and obtaining a final adjudication as to whether the will is genuine or not. It was held in that case that the heirs of the sole legatee were entitled to letters of Administration under section 233 of the Succession Act without any question being raised as to their competency. These divergence rulings were reviewed by a learned Single Judge in the case of Jadeja Pravin-sinhji Vs. Jadeja Mangnisinhji and others A.I.R. 1953 Guzrat 32. It was held that an executor named in the win and who may happen to be a beneficiary under the will, in applying for probate does not fight a personal action but fights for the interests of all the beneficiaries under the will. Therefore the action of an executor in applying for a probate is not in substance a personal action In case of his demise pending the probate proceedings the maxim action personalis moritur cum persona does not apply. On the death of the executor, the action which he started does not come to an end. Any of those whom he was representing are entitled to intervene and carry on the proceedings with a modification by way of an amendment praying the court to grant letters of administration with the will annexed. 

 "The proceedings of the Court of the District Judge in relation to the granting of probate and letters of administration snail, save as hereinafter otherwise provided, be regulated, so far as the circumstances of the case permit, by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. 

 This section is very wide but is hedged by the limitation "save as hereinafter otherwise provided." This section makes applicable the procedural provision of the Code of Civil Procedure to the proceeding under the Succession Act in relating to the granting of Probate and letter of Administration. Section 222 precedes section 268. It therefore does not come within the mischief of the saving clause as hereinafter otherwise provided."Illustration (i) to section 222 makes the position clear. A will that C be his executor if B wills not B is appointed executor by implication. And that is covered by sub-section (1). Again a persons who though not expressly appointed as executor, is directed to receive and pay the testator's debts and to get in and distribute his personal estate, must be taken to have been appointed under the will as executor by implication. This is covered by sub-section (2). This proposition is supported by the decision in the matter of Monohar Mukherjee: 5 Cal 756. To take section 222 in its absolute term will be erroneous. Such provisions confer a faculty or power but they do not follow by such words as that anything done contrary to these provisions shall be null and void to all intents'. Such is the legislative practice whenever it is considered to confer a power in absolute terms. Section 222 is not such a provision. An enabling provision without a contrary clause cannot be viewed as a bar. The learned Judges of the High Court Division had fallen into error on this point.
